world.era: 1760s-2014 (case studies across history; frame is present-day)
world.setting: A present-day deep dive that visits the labs, studios and streets where expertise was measured: a 1970s Carnegie Mellon memory lab, a Tokyo music school, Bell Labs, a weekend tennis court, hospitals, a ballet studio, London's streets and MRI lab, a 1924 New York chess exhibition, a Berlin music academy, a Hamburg club, a modern office.

objects.why: Steve Faloon's trick: he turned digit strings into cross-country running times (9:07 = a two-mile time); also the one-digit-per-second pacing of the lab.
The Tokyo perfect-pitch study (toddlers naming chords) and Mozart's training; no shared icon draws a keyboard.
The book's core mechanism: the brain physically rebuilds itself (myelin, the cabbies' hippocampus, shrinking after retirement). Shared icons have no brain.
Naive practice: the weekend tennis player who plays 20 years and never gets better.
Franklin's 50 years of naive chess, Alekhine's 26 blindfold games, Simon's real vs random boards; the shared game icon is not a chessboard.
The music lesson that shows naive practice ('I just played it').
The ballet dancers' 10,000 hours of instructor-led studio practice: deliberate practice in its purest form.
The London taxi drivers learning The Knowledge, whose hippocampus grew; the shared car is a generic car.
The Berlin violin study behind the 10,000-hour myth; mustSee: a child practicing violin.
Franklin rewriting Spectator essays and marking his failures in red ink: feedback, the self-made coach, 'seek out the red ink'.
Turock's 'learning while real work gets done': videotape your presentation and have a critic tear it apart.
Steve's retrieval structure: a tree with fixed branches the digits hang on.
The edge of ability: practice at the edge of failure.
The myth of the innate gift (talent as a present you are born with).

spine.claim: An ordinary student goes from 8 to 82 digits: experts are not born with a gift - the body and brain adapt to whatever hard demand you place on them (Tokyo toddlers learn perfect pitch, Mozart was trained, Paul Brady trained it at 32).

Steve built a retrieval structure and rebuilt it at every plateau, while naive practice - the tennis player, Franklin's 50 years of chess, veteran doctors - locks you in once a skill turns automatic: comfort is where improvement stops.

Deliberate practice (a teacher, a specific goal, immediate feedback, a demand just past your ability) physically rebuilds the brain - the cabbies' hippocampus grows and shrinks back when they stop - and builds mental representations that let experts see what novices can't (Alekhine, the mechanic, the diagnostician, Simon's chessboards).

The 10,000-hour rule bends the Berlin violin study: hours in your comfort zone guarantee nothing; outside structured fields you must build your own feedback loops (Franklin's red ink, radiologists without feedback, Turock's videotaped rehearsal).

Genes set physical limits, but mental 'talent' is mostly a story told after the fact: the question is never 'do I have the gift?' but 'where is my edge, and am I standing on it?' - and what if society trained everyone instead of scouting talent?
